label: clean
notes: Authenticated third-party service mail. Trusted-domain match is a signal, not proof of safety.

label: spam
notes: Legitimate marketing someone over-reported. Header signals resolve this at near-zero false-positive cost, where Enron-trained models measured a 0.959 false-positive rate.

label: threat
notes: The case that defeated both LFM and FraudFoxAI in the predecessor's testing. Deterministic lookalike detection catches it.

label: threat
notes: Visible text advertises the protected domain; the href goes elsewhere. This is why links must be parsed from markup rather than read as text.

label: threat
notes: Destination hidden behind a URL-rewriting proxy. The reference playbook asks an LLM to percent-decode this; it is deterministic.

label: threat
notes: A user forwarded a phish to the helpdesk. The outer From is the reporting user and must not be judged as the sender.

label: threat
notes: Macro-bearing document from an external sender. Only the MIME inventory is asserted here; content extraction is a separate stage.

label: threat
notes: Message content attempting to steer the analysis pipeline. The predecessor engine had no guard for this at all; the reference relies on the model resisting it. We detect and record the attempt.

label: threat
notes: Business email compromise shape: authentication passes, there is no suspicious link, and the only evidence is the request itself. This is the case the reference playbook's domain-match rule gets wrong, and the one that must reach the adjudication tier rather than being auto-cleared by deterministic rules.

label: clean
notes: A legitimate security newsletter that QUOTES prompt-injection phrases while discussing them. The deterministic scanner fires on this, and that is the point: it must not become a THREAT verdict. Distinguishing 'contains an instruction aimed at an agent' from 'quotes an instruction while discussing it' is not something a regex can do reliably. Horizon-Labs' own card lists discussing prompt injection as a non-injection. A university SOC subscribes to exactly these newsletters.

label: clean
notes: The counter-fixture for the redirect-concealment rule: passing authentication, a legitimate external sender, and a link to a domain that matches neither the sender nor the trusted list -- with no wrapper hiding it. The reference playbook's prompt calls a destination mismatch "a very strong indicator of a threat"; mail to unrelated services is ordinary, so a mismatch must not be decisive in either direction. If this dispositions as anything but clean, the rule keyed on mismatch instead of on concealment.

label: threat
notes: Credential harvesting drawn in pixels: the login form is an inline image part with a Content-ID, so there is no anchor to analyse and nothing for text scanning to match. Parity gaps 5 and 6 in docs/PARITY.md. Asset sha256 2b129bc3fd9fcfc2cd36b998166c30f2a637c48df7c1894743640f040ccdb510.
